description: Can a human voice break a wine glass, with no speaker? We test three cases on the same crystal glass: the wrong note sung loud, the right note sung quietly, then the right note sung loud.
The wrong note barely moves the glass. The right note sung quietly makes the rim wobble, but it holds. The right note sung loud makes the rim bend more and more until the glass shatters.

Why: every glass has its own note, its resonant frequency (tap it and you hear it). When a voice holds exactly that note, each vibration of the air pushes the rim at the right moment, so the bending adds up cycle after cycle. Any other note pushes at the wrong moments and the effect cancels out. Unamplified, it takes upward of 100 decibels.

MythBusters tested it in 2005 (episode 31, 'Breaking Glass'): singer Jaime Vendera broke a lead crystal glass with his unamplified voice, registered at 105 dB, after trying 12 wine glasses before one shattered (Scientific American).
This video is a 3D simulation (Blender). The bending of the rim is exaggerated so it can be seen; the real movement is a fraction of a millimetre.
sources_detail: MythBusters, episode 31 'Breaking Glass' (Discovery, 18 May 2005): myth confirmed; Jaime Vendera broke a lead crystal glass with his unaided voice (mythresults.com/episode31).

Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction?: An Opera Singer's Piercing Voice Can Shatter Glass': without amplification it takes upward of 100 decibels; Vendera's shot registered at 105 decibels; he tried 12 wine glasses before one shattered; the matching pitch is the glass's resonant frequency (can be any note).

On screen: 105 dB (round 1 and 3, as measured by MythBusters), 'under 100 dB' for the quiet round (below the threshold given by Scientific American). Simulated: rim motion (first bending mode, exaggerated), timings, shard motion.
